passages.title: Teenagers and sleep
passages.body: Adolescents need around nine hours of sleep, {{1}} most of them get considerably less. School start times are partly to blame; many students must wake at six, {{2}} their biological clocks shift later during puberty. A study {{3}} followed several thousand teenagers found that those who slept less performed worse on attention tests. When one district delayed the start of classes by an hour, attendance improved {{4}} a measurable rise in test scores. Critics note that later start times can interfere {{5}} after-school sports and part-time jobs, but supporters argue that health should take priority. Researchers have therefore suggested that the problem is structural rather than personal, and that families alone cannot solve it.

passages.title: The year without a summer
passages.body: Volcanic eruptions can influence the global climate {{1}} they inject ash and sulphur gases high into the atmosphere. In 1815, the eruption of Mount Tambora, {{2}} was the largest in recorded history, lowered temperatures worldwide, and 1816 became known as the year without a summer. Crops failed in Europe and North America, {{3}} food prices rose sharply. Before satellites existed, scientists had to rely on historical records to reconstruct such events. Since the 1970s, however, satellites {{4}} researchers with continuous data on volcanic activity. Today, this monitoring allows scientists to {{5}} the spread of volcanic gases within days, and to warn aviation authorities when ash clouds threaten flights.

passages.title: How printing changed society
passages.body: The introduction of the printing press transformed European society. {{1}} books had once been copied by hand and were affordable only to the wealthy, printed texts became cheap enough for ordinary families. Literacy rates rose, and the demand for schools grew {{2}} a result. Governments soon realized that an educated population was good for trade, and they began to invest {{3}} public education. Not everyone welcomed the change, however. Some authorities feared that cheap books would spread dangerous ideas, so they introduced systems to {{4}} publications before they were sold. Historians now agree that the printing press was {{5}} important for the spread of science than any single invention before it.

passages.title: Glaciers and water supplies
passages.body: Glaciers store about two thirds of the world's fresh water, {{1}} their melting has consequences far beyond mountain regions. Meltwater initially increases river flows, which can benefit farmers; {{2}}, once the ice has largely gone, flows decline sharply. Communities in the Andes and the Himalayas, {{3}} depend on glacial rivers during the dry season, are already adapting. So far, engineers {{4}} artificial ice stupas that store winter water until spring, and several villages have built small reservoirs. Whether such measures will be enough remains {{5}}, since the rate of melting continues to accelerate in many regions.

passages.title: Handwashing and Semmelweis
passages.body: In the nineteenth century, a Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that women {{1}} gave birth in one hospital ward died far more often than those in another. He eventually concluded that doctors, some of {{2}} had come directly from autopsies, were carrying infection on their hands. When he required them to wash with chlorinated lime, mortality fell dramatically. Had his colleagues accepted the evidence, thousands of lives {{3}} saved. His ideas were vindicated only after Pasteur and Lister had {{4}} the germ theory of disease. Today, hand washing is regarded as one of the most cost-effective health measures, precisely {{5}} it is so simple.

passages.title: Remote work after 2020
passages.body: Remote work, once a rare privilege, became widespread almost overnight in 2020. Employees {{1}} commuting times had been long welcomed the change, but others missed the social contact of the office. Surveys suggest that productivity depends largely {{2}} the type of task: individual work often improves at home, {{3}} collaborative projects tend to suffer. Many firms now adopt hybrid schedules, {{4}} staff spend some days in the office and others at home. If managers {{5}} more flexibility earlier, they might have avoided the sudden disruption that followed, and workers would have had more time to adjust to the new arrangements.

passages.title: Artificial photosynthesis
passages.body: Plants convert sunlight into chemical energy with an efficiency of only about one percent, so researchers have long hoped to build systems that do better. Artificial photosynthesis devices split water into hydrogen and oxygen, and the hydrogen can then be {{1}} as a clean fuel. Early prototypes were {{2}} unstable that they lasted only a few hours. Recent designs, {{3}} use cheap catalysts instead of platinum, have operated for weeks. Still, the technology is unlikely to compete with fossil fuels {{4}} costs fall further. Even then, engineers will have to {{5}} the problem of storing and transporting hydrogen safely, which remains a major obstacle for the whole industry.
